title: Act II, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: After midnight Banquo, unable to sleep, tells Fleance of 'cursed thoughts' and gives Macbeth a diamond from the king for Lady Macbeth. Banquo mentions dreaming of the Witches; Macbeth claims he does not think of them and hints at future honor if Banquo will 'cleave to my consent'; Banquo agrees only if he keeps his allegiance clear. Alone, Macbeth sees a dagger in the air leading him to Duncan, wonders if it is 'a dagger of the mind', and goes when the bell rings: 'Hear it not, Duncan; for it is a knell.'

context.history: Plays at the Globe were performed in daylight, so night had to be created by words: references to darkness, torches and the bell signal the hour.

significance: The dagger soliloquy dramatizes a mind dividing against itself; whether the dagger is supernatural or hallucinated is left open, and the play keeps asking whether what Macbeth sees is real.
discussionQuestions: Have you ever been so anxious or guilty that you imagined something that was not there?
Where does imagery appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with appearance versus reality?

anchorPassages.note: First half of the dagger soliloquy: hallucination as conscience and lure.
anchorPassages.text:
Is this a dagger which I see before me,
The handle toward my hand? Come, let me clutch thee.
I have thee not, and yet I see thee still.
Art thou not, fatal vision, sensible
To feeling as to sight? or art thou but
A dagger of the mind, a false creation,
Proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain?
I see thee yet, in form as palpable
As this which now I draw.
Thou marshall’st me the way that I was going;
And such an instrument I was to use.
Mine eyes are made the fools o’ the other senses,
Or else worth all the rest; I see thee still,
And on thy blade and dudgeon gouts of blood,
Which was not so before. There’s no such thing:
It is the bloody business which informs
Thus to mine eyes. Now o’er the one half-world
Nature seems dead, and wicked dreams abuse

weDoAnswers: "Heat-oppressed brain" means a feverish mind: the vision is guilt. Expected link: guilt and conscience.
analysis.weDoWords: “Dagger of the mind”, “false creation” and “heat-oppressed” stand out. Macbeth tells himself the dagger is not real, only the product of a fevered, overheated brain.
analysis.weDoQ2: The dagger appears before any murder, so the line shows guilt at work in advance: Macbeth's conscience pictures the deed before his hand does it.

segments.script: Today's words: dudgeon — the handle of a dagger; allegiance — loyalty owed to a ruler; husbandry — thrift; careful saving; palpable — able to be touched or felt; augment — to increase. “allegiance”: Origin: Anglo-Norman alegaunce. “husbandry”: Origin: an English formation from husband + -ry. “palpable”: Origin: Middle French palpable; earlier Latin palpābilis. “augment”: Origin: Middle French augmenter; earlier Old French augmenter.

words.sentence:
Mine eyes are made the fools o’ the other senses,
Or else worth all the rest; I see thee still,
And on thy blade and dudgeon gouts of blood,
Which was not so before.

So I lose none
In seeking to augment it, but still keep
My bosom franchised and allegiance clear,
I shall be counsell’d.

There’s husbandry in heaven;
Their candles are all out.

As this which now I draw.

So I lose none

segments.script: Plays at the Globe were performed in daylight, so night had to be created by words: references to darkness, torches and the bell signal the hour. The dagger soliloquy dramatizes a mind dividing against itself; whether the dagger is supernatural or hallucinated is left open, and the play keeps asking whether what Macbeth sees is real. Soliloquy: The dagger speech: Macbeth sees a dagger "of the mind," then real blood on it; he cannot tell imagination from reality. Dialogue: Banquo admits dreaming of the weird sisters; Macbeth lies ("I think not of them") and hints at reward for support. Imagery: Night, witchcraft, Tarquin's "ravishing strides": the world of the murder. Watch for the prophecies: The Witches' riddling prophecies: notice how each promise shapes what Macbeth hopes, fears and does next.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Is this a dagger which I see before me, / The handle toward my hand” slowly and put it in my own words: Alone before the murder, Macbeth sees a dagger floating in the air, its handle toward his hand. Next, craft. I notice the question he asks himself, which shows he cannot tell what is real. The strongest word is “dagger”: it is the weapon he is about to use, now appearing as a vision. Then, effect. What does the dagger vision show about Macbeth's mind? My answer: His mind is already guilty and disturbed; the dagger leads him toward Duncan's room, as if his imagination is pulling him into the crime.

segments.script: Ask: What words in this line stand out, and what do they suggest? Expected student answer: “Dagger of the mind”, “false creation” and “heat-oppressed” stand out. segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the scene for soliloquy, dialogue (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about the dagger of the mind? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Act II, Scene I develops the idea of the dagger of the mind. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: The dagger speech shows that Macbeth's conscience is already tormenting him before he kills. When the text says “A dagger of the mind, a false creation, / Proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain” (Act II, Scene I, lines 620–621), it shows this directly. He calls it "a dagger of the mind, a false creation, / Proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain," knowing his imagination is creating the weapon, yet he follows it: "I go, and it is done."

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
